subject: Climate & Environment
title: Coral Reefs Under Acid Stress
description: A micro-lesson that makes Coral Reefs Under Acid Stress usable.

hook.text: Corals build their skeletons from calcium carbonate. Acidification makes that harder every year.

buildup.text: Reefs already face bleaching from heat. Acidification adds a second, simultaneous threat.

discovery.text: Under more acidic conditions, corals grow slower and their skeletons become brittle and porous.

twist.text: At a pH of 7.8 — possible by 2100 — coral reefs would dissolve faster than they can grow.

climax.text: Losing reefs means losing the 25% of marine species that depend on them for survival.

punchline.text: Heat bleaches them. Acid dissolves them. Corals are under siege from both sides.

quiz.question: What is the combined threat to coral reefs from warming and acidification?
options: Heat bleaches corals while acid weakens their skeletons
Both cause corals to grow faster

details.summary: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor yet support about 25 percent of all marine species. Acidification makes it harder for corals to deposit calcium carbonate skeletons, slowing growth and weakening reef structure while warming triggers mass bleaching events.
details.whyItMatters: Coral reefs protect coastlines, sustain fisheries, and support tourism worth billions of dollars. Losing them would devastate marine biodiversity and coastal economies.
takeaways: Reefs support roughly 25 percent of marine species
Acidification slows coral skeleton growth and weakens reefs
Warming causes mass bleaching that can kill entire reef systems

faq.question: What is coral bleaching?
faq.answer: Bleaching occurs when stressed corals expel symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae that provide them with food and color. Without these algae, corals turn white and begin to starve. If conditions persist, the coral dies.

faq.question: Can coral reefs recover from bleaching?
faq.answer: If temperatures return to normal quickly, corals can reabsorb algae and recover over several years. However, repeated bleaching events now occur faster than reefs can regenerate, causing cumulative decline worldwide.
